sm: The show opens with the news from Kent Covington. President Trump says the U.S. is investigating reports, carried by CNN, that Iran may be plotting a major attack in Washington, possibly with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon aimed at top officials. Intelligence officials disagree about whether Iran could carry it out, Iran calls the report baseless, and the White House says it has no evidence of a credible threat to the homeland. Trump, in the Philippines, said Thailand agreed to drop tariffs on American goods and buy billions in farm products, and he met leaders from Australia, India and Japan, who announced joint maritime patrols and cooperation on artificial intelligence. He is expected to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China tomorrow. House Democrats vote today and Hakeem Jeffries is running unopposed for Speaker, while Senate Democrats vote December first on a leadership race in which Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from Chris Van Hollen, who wants to end the filibuster. Jeffries also demanded answers about recent outages involving air traffic control, Microsoft, banking, the NSA network and Apple, none of which officials blame on cyber attacks.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy asked Senate Republicans for another fifty billion dollars to overhaul aging air traffic control systems. Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia chief executive last week amid a scandal over an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, will answer questions from three House committees behind closed doors on December first about chip sales to China. More than one hundred ninety thousand people, including Elon Musk, signed a petition urging the board not to rush to replace him, though Reuters reports the board is not considering bringing him back. The program then turns to Washington Wednesday with political scientist Hunter Baker. Discussing last Friday's nearly five hour nationwide ground stop, Baker says mid-century America could carry out huge projects like the interstate highways and the TVA, but today it cannot, despite better technology. He blames weak political will and attention, and the FAA for updating terminals rather than air traffic control, which Congress ordered modernized in 2003. He adds that protests, lawsuits and people profiting from delays make big projects harder, and that politics has become dominated by show rather than delivery.

The hosts turn to tomorrow's expected meeting of Trump with Putin and Xi Jinping, with arms control, Ukraine and Iran on the agenda. Baker says talking is better than not talking, but Ukraine and Taiwan should be nervous because Trump is weakened. He expects China to seek a statement that American commitment to Taiwan is reduced, and Ukrainians to worry Trump will press them to cede territory. The U.S. also wants help from Russia and China on Iran. Next, they discuss a Wall Street Journal piece arguing Pat Buchanan anticipated Trump's tariffs, immigration policy and populism. Baker says the end of the Cold War broke the glue holding the Republican coalition together, and that Trump is essentially Buchanan two point oh. In the lightning round, Baker says Senator John Cornyn's fight over the blue slip tradition is one the Senate should let go. He rates New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's disbanding of the NYPD protest unit a six out of ten for risk to public safety, calling it a step toward defunding police.

Baker finishes by saying the NSA outage, coming right after the FAA shutdown, is worrisome because technology creates new vulnerabilities, and that the country needs a next president with the competence and attention to focus on it. World Tour then reports on human trafficking into scam compounds in Southeast Asia. The United Nations estimates more than three hundred thousand people from about eighty countries have been trafficked to compounds mostly in Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos. Victims are lured by fake job ads, have passports confiscated, and are abused and forced to run online scams. A nineteen year old Ethiopian man says he was shocked and punched daily. Myanmar freed over nine thousand victims last year after pressure from China and Thailand. Amy Miller of Acts Mercy says survivors are sometimes treated as immigration violators in Thailand, and cuts to U.S. funding for the UN migration agency made repatriation harder. Acts Mercy helped raise almost two hundred twenty three thousand dollars for over three thousand freed workers.

Ever Free's Uganda director says survivors' top needs are physical health and household income, and the group offers healthcare and vocational programs. Andrew Wasuwong of International Justice Mission in Thailand says survivors struggle with guilt, flashbacks and nightmares, and need counseling and peer networks, and some have started their own groups to warn others. The show then shares a light story about Chicago and St. Louis rivals failing to push the Bean sculpture and the Gateway Arch. The next feature, from Mary Reichard, looks at growing demand for cosmetic procedures, which rose nearly a quarter among adults over sixty five last year. Christian writer Laurie Higgins drew a huge response when she questioned cosmetic surgery on Facebook, and many conservative women defended it. Philosopher Heather Widdows says procedures like Botox are starting to feel obligatory, and that women are judged either as vain or as letting themselves go.

Higgins says the church has been largely silent as beauty culture shifted from cosmetics toward costly, invasive procedures to hold back aging. She says this raises Christian questions about what our bodies are for, who they belong to, how to steward money, and what older women teach younger ones. Widdows is hesitant to blame people, since selfie culture makes appearance matter. Higgins urges Christian women to place their identity elsewhere, saying her job is to live rightly. Part two airs tomorrow. Commentator Cal Thomas then asks why Democrats cannot settle on who should live or die with the state's help. He notes California Governor Gavin Newsom plans to commute more than five hundred death sentences to life without parole, while New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed an assisted suicide law. Thomas calls her wording Orwellian and warns that pressure could eventually fall on the elderly, as it has in Canada. Tomorrow's show covers Roblox and child safety, and part two of the aging story.
